ai.title: Add CLI rage detection system
ai.summary: Implements rage detection in `npm-app` CLI via new `rage-detectors.ts` and `utils/rage-detector.ts`. Tracks key mashing, repeat inputs, exits after errors, and hangs (spinner, commands, WebSocket) using count, time-between, and timeout strategies. Fires `cli.rage` analytics event defined in `common/src/constants/analytics-events.ts`. Integrates into `npm-app/src/cli.ts` and refactors `npm-app/src/utils/spinner.ts` to use the new detector.

eli5.text: The app now watches for signs that you're frustrated and quietly records when it happens, without showing you anything new on screen. For example, if you bang out five or more keystrokes within one second, enter the same command three times within thirty seconds, quit right after an error appears within ten seconds, or wait over a minute while the loading spinner is stuck, the app logs a private 'rage' event to help the makers understand what's going wrong. You won't see a pop-up or message from this, but the team building the app can use these logs to fix the spots that make you want to smash your keyboard. This is live today for everyone using the app.

ai.title: Global rage detector singleton and flexible time-between operators
ai.summary: Introduced a global `rageDetectors` singleton in `npm-app/src/rage-detectors.ts`, replacing per-CLI-instance initialization to enable application-wide access. Enhanced `createTimeBetweenDetector` in `npm-app/src/utils/rage-detector.ts` to support configurable comparison operators (`lt`, `gt`, `eq`, `gte`, `lte`), defaulting to `lt` for backward compatibility. Added `startupTimeDetector` and `exitTimeDetector` with `gte` thresholds to track slow startup and exit sequences in `npm-app/src/index.ts`. Updated `npm-app/src/cli.ts` to reference the singleton for error, hang, and repeat input detection.

eli5.text: The app now watches for itself getting stuck during two specific moments: when it first starts up and when it shuts down. Previously, only one part of the program could check whether things were taking too long, but now a single set of timers is shared across the entire app, so any piece of it can start, stop, or reset these checks. For example, if starting up takes more than 5 seconds or shutting down takes more than 10 seconds, the app will notice and can flag that as a problem. Anyone running the app in a terminal may see these new slow-startup and slow-exit warnings appear where they previously did not.

If you install the assistant today, it can now detect when a conversation is going off the rails and flag it to whoever is running the system. This detection is new in version 1.0.334, which also includes faster checkpoint saving, a spinner that notices and recovers from hangs, and the removal of an old CI workflow that is no longer needed. You would not see this yourself, but the system behind the assistant now notices and reacts to rage events automatically. None of this changes what you can ask the assistant; it only changes how reliably the assistant behaves.
